tagline: A short letter from Paul to Titus on Crete about appointing faithful elders, silencing false teachers, and the good works that grace produces.
overview:
Titus is a brief letter of instruction to one of Paul's most trusted coworkers, left on the island of Crete to put the young churches there in order. Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town, men of proven character who hold firmly to sound teaching, because the churches were troubled by rebellious teachers, many from a Jewish background, who were upsetting whole households for the sake of money. He then tells Titus what to teach older men and women, younger men and women, and slaves, and why.

The why is the heart of the letter. Twice Paul grounds his practical instructions in compact summaries of the gospel: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone and training believers to live godly lives as they wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:11-14); and when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, he saved us not because of our righteous deeds but by his mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit (3:4-7). Good works are not the root of salvation but its fruit, and the letter uses the phrase good works or good deeds again and again.

Titus is closely related to 1 Timothy in subject and vocabulary, and together with 2 Timothy it forms the group called the Pastoral Letters. It is shorter and more compact than 1 Timothy, and some of its gospel summaries are among the richest in the New Testament.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author (1:1) and was received by the church as his. It appears in the Muratorian list of the late second century, and early writers such as Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria quote it. The second-century teacher Marcion did not include it, or the other Pastoral Letters, in his collection of Paul's letters.

The authorship debate over the Pastoral Letters applies fully to Titus (see the introduction to 1 Timothy). Scholars who think a later follower of Paul wrote it point to vocabulary and style that differ from Paul's undisputed letters, to a church order with elders appointed in every town, to a false teaching they associate with a later period, and to the difficulty of fitting a mission on Crete into the story of Acts, which mentions Crete only as a place Paul sailed past as a prisoner (Acts 27:7-13). Scholars who hold that Paul wrote it answer that differences of style reflect a different kind of letter and subject; that appointing elders was Paul's practice from his first missionary trip (Acts 14:23); that the Jewish myths and quarrels about the law fit the first century; and that a mission on Crete fits the period after Paul's first Roman imprisonment, if he was released as early tradition reports. Mediating views suggest a secretary given freedom in wording or a later editor working with Paul's own notes. Evangelical scholarship generally holds to Paul's authorship; a majority of critical scholars do not.
date: If Paul wrote the letter, it most likely comes from the same period as 1 Timothy, after his release from house arrest in Rome, around AD 62 to 64. Paul had evidently worked on Crete with Titus and left him there, and at the time of writing he planned to spend the winter at Nicopolis (3:12). A few scholars have tried to place the letter earlier, within the period covered by Acts, but the details fit awkwardly. Scholars who see the letter as written by a later follower of Paul usually date it between about AD 80 and 110.
setting:
Crete is a large, mountainous island in the Mediterranean, south of the Aegean Sea. It had been home to the Minoan civilization in the second millennium BC, and by the first century it was part of a Roman province that joined Crete with Cyrene on the North African coast. It had a substantial Jewish population, and Cretans were among those present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). The island also had a poor reputation in the Greek world for dishonesty and greed, which Paul acknowledges by quoting a Cretan poet traditionally identified as Epimenides (1:12).

Titus was a Gentile convert whom Paul had taken to Jerusalem and whom the apostles did not require to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3). He had served as Paul's representative to the troubled church in Corinth, where he handled difficult matters with success (2 Corinthians 7:6-15; 8:16-23). His task on Crete was to set in order what was unfinished (1:5), a young and loosely organized set of congregations in several towns, some of them unsettled by teachers who emphasized Jewish myths, genealogies, and quarrels about the law. Later Titus went to Dalmatia, on the eastern coast of the Adriatic (2 Timothy 4:10).
purpose: Paul writes to authorize and guide Titus in organizing the churches of Crete. He wants qualified elders appointed so that the churches can resist false teachers; he wants Titus to teach each group within the church how to live in a way that commends the gospel to outsiders; and he wants believers to devote themselves to good works, to be good citizens, and to avoid divisive controversy. The letter also carries practical arrangements: Titus is to join Paul at Nicopolis once a replacement arrives, and to help Zenas and Apollos on their way.
story: Titus belongs to the last stage of Paul's story, after the events recorded in Acts, when Paul was establishing leaders to carry on his work. Like 1 Timothy, it shows the transition from the apostolic founding of churches to their ongoing life under local leaders. In the New Testament it stands between 2 Timothy and Philemon, the last of the letters traditionally grouped under Paul's name before Hebrews.
christ: Titus calls both God and Jesus Christ Savior, sometimes in the same breath (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4-6), and it contains one of the New Testament's clearest statements of Christ's deity in most translations: the glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:13). Christ gave himself to redeem a people from lawlessness and to purify them for himself (2:14). Through him the Holy Spirit was poured out, so that those justified by grace become heirs of eternal life (3:6-7). The appearing of God's grace in Christ's first coming and the appearing of his glory at his return frame the whole Christian life.
reading: Read Titus as a companion to 1 Timothy and notice the differences as well as the likenesses: here the churches are younger, the instruction more basic, and the concern for outsiders' opinion very strong. Watch for the phrase good works, which recurs throughout, and for the purpose clauses that explain Paul's instructions, so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5) and so that believers will adorn the teaching about God (2:10). Some of the letter's instructions reflect household structures of the Roman world, and readers should consider how the principle underneath them applies today. Contested questions, especially about elders' qualifications, deserve a fair hearing of more than one view.

structure.title: Greeting
structure.summary: An unusually full opening in which Paul describes his apostleship in terms of the faith of God's elect and the hope of eternal life.

structure.title: Elders and false teachers
structure.summary: Titus is to appoint elders of proven character who hold to sound teaching, because rebellious teachers must be silenced and rebuked.

structure.title: Teaching for every household
structure.summary: Instructions for older and younger men and women, for Titus himself, and for slaves, grounded in the grace of God that trains believers to live godly lives as they await Christ's appearing.

structure.title: Good citizens saved by mercy
structure.summary: Believers are to be gentle and ready for good works toward all, because God saved them by his mercy through new birth and the Holy Spirit; they must avoid foolish controversies.

structure.title: Travel plans and greetings
structure.summary: Paul asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis, to help Zenas and Apollos, and to teach believers to meet pressing needs.

themes.title: Grace that trains
themes.body: The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and it instructs believers to renounce ungodliness and live upright lives (2:11-12). In Titus, grace is not only pardon but training. It saves and it shapes, and the two cannot be separated.

themes.title: Good works
themes.body: The phrase good works or good deeds, and related expressions, run through every chapter. False teachers are unfit for any good deed (1:16); Titus must model good works (2:7); Christ purified a people zealous for good deeds (2:14); believers must be ready for every good work (3:1) and devote themselves to meeting pressing needs (3:14). Good works do not earn salvation (3:5) but display it.

themes.title: The gospel and outsiders
themes.body: Paul repeatedly explains his instructions by their effect on those outside the church: so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5), so that opponents will have nothing bad to say (2:8), so that slaves may adorn the teaching (2:10). Christian conduct in ordinary roles makes the gospel attractive or repellent to neighbors.

themes.title: God our Savior
themes.body: Titus uses the title Savior six times, three of God and three of Jesus Christ, often in close pairs. The letter's two great gospel summaries (2:11-14 and 3:4-7) describe salvation as the work of the Father's kindness, the Son's self-giving, and the Spirit's renewal.

themes.title: Sound teaching and leadership
themes.body: As in 1 Timothy, sound, healthy teaching is set against empty talk, myths, and quarrels. Elders must hold firmly to the faithful word so that they can encourage believers and refute those who contradict it (1:9).

keyChapters.why: Sets out the qualifications of elders on Crete and describes the false teachers they must resist.
Grounds instructions for every group in the church in the grace of God that trains believers, and names Jesus Christ our great God and Savior.
Contains one of the New Testament's fullest summaries of salvation by mercy through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.

parts.body:
Titus is a short letter from Paul to Titus, one of his most trusted fellow workers, whom he had left on the island of Crete. It has 3 chapters and can be read aloud in about eight minutes.

The churches on Crete were young and unfinished. They had no appointed leaders, and some teachers were upsetting whole households for money. Paul gives Titus three tasks. Appoint elders in every town, people of tested character who hold to the true teaching (1:5-9). Stop the teachers who are doing harm (1:10-16). And teach every part of the church, old and young, men and women, slave and free, how to live in a way that makes the gospel attractive (chapter 2 and 3:1-2).

The letter is practical, but twice it opens up into a short, rich summary of the gospel. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone” (2:11), and that grace trains us to live well while we wait for Christ. And “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy” (3:5).

One phrase runs through all three chapters: good works. They do not save anyone; the letter says so plainly (3:5). But people who have been saved by mercy are to be ‘zealous for good deeds’ (2:14). In Titus, what you believe always shows up in how you live.

Some passages in Titus are hard and have been misused: the saying about Cretans (1:12), the words to wives (2:5) and to slaves (2:9-10). These notes face them honestly, set out the main readings fairly, and take no side where faithful Christians differ.

The letter opens with Paul's name (1:1) and was received by the church as his. It is in the Muratorian list of the late second century, and early writers such as Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria quote it. Marcion, a second-century teacher whose views the church rejected, did not include it, or the other Pastoral Letters, in his collection of Paul's letters.

Titus belongs with 1 and 2 Timothy, the three Pastoral Letters, and the question of who wrote them is asked of all three together. The book page on 1 Timothy sets it out in the part ‘Who wrote it: the Pastoral Letters’: why many scholars have concluded that a later follower of Paul wrote them in his name, and why many others hold that Paul wrote them. Both views are held by careful scholars, and readers on both sides take the letters as Scripture. These notes do not choose, and they speak of the writer as Paul, as the letter does.

One point bears on Titus in particular. Acts never tells of Paul working on Crete. Scholars who hold that Paul wrote the letter place his work there after the end of Acts, if he was released from his first imprisonment in Rome, as early writers report. Scholars who think a later follower wrote it see the setting as part of the letter's picture of Paul.

Crete is a large, mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, south of the Aegean. In Paul's day it was joined with Cyrene, on the coast of North Africa, as one Roman province. It had several cities and a Jewish community: the Jewish writer Philo mentions Jews on Crete, and Cretans were among the crowd in Jerusalem at Pentecost who heard the apostles speak (Acts 2:11).

Here it helps to be clear about what we know. Acts mentions Crete only once, when Paul sailed past it as a prisoner on his way to Rome. His ship sheltered at a harbour called Fair Havens on the south coast, and Paul warned the crew not to sail on, but they did, and ran into a great storm (Acts 27:7-13). Acts does not tell of Paul preaching on Crete or starting churches there.

The letter itself says that Paul left Titus in Crete to finish the work (1:5), which means Paul had been there with him. If Paul wrote the letter, this most likely happened after Acts ends, if he was released from house arrest in Rome, around AD 62 to 64. At the time of writing, Paul planned to spend the winter at Nicopolis, a city on the western coast of Greece founded by Augustus to mark his victory at Actium in 31 BC (3:12), and most scholars think that is the Nicopolis he meant.

Crete also had a poor name among other Greeks. They said Cretans lied, and Paul quotes a Cretan poet who said so (1:12). The part on that saying below explains why it is no licence for contempt.

Titus was a Gentile, not a Jew. Paul calls him ‘my true child in our common faith’ (1:4). Years earlier Paul had taken him to Jerusalem, and the leaders there did not make him be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3). He became a living sign that Gentiles belong to God's people through faith in Christ, without becoming Jews first.

Paul trusted him with hard tasks. He sent him to the troubled church in Corinth, and Titus came back with good news that comforted Paul (2 Corinthians 7:6-7). He helped gather the gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8:6, 16-17).

Now Paul had left him on Crete to put things in order. Later, in 2 Timothy, we hear that Titus had gone to Dalmatia, on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea (2 Timothy 4:10). Titus is never mentioned in Acts.

Greeting (1:1-4). One of Paul's longest openings, full of faith, truth, godliness and ‘the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began’ (1:2).

Elders and false teachers (1:5-16). Appoint elders of tested character who hold to sound teaching. Silence the teachers who upset households for money.

Teaching for every household (2:1-15). What older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself and slaves are to be like, so that the gospel is honoured. Then the reason: the grace of God has appeared, and it trains us as we wait for ‘our great God and Savior Jesus Christ’ (2:13).

Good citizens saved by mercy (3:1-11). Be gentle and ready for good works toward everyone, because we too were once lost, and God saved us by his mercy. Avoid pointless quarrels; warn a divisive person.

Plans and greetings (3:12-15). Come to me at Nicopolis; help Zenas and Apollos on their way; learn to meet pressing needs.

Titus is to ‘appoint elders in every town’ (1:5). Paul had done the same from his first missionary trip (Acts 14:23). In verse 7 he calls the same leader an ‘overseer’, so in this letter the two words seem to name the same people.

Almost everything on the list is about character. An elder must be ‘blameless’ in his home. As ‘God's steward’, the manager of a household on its owner's behalf, he must not be ‘self-absorbed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money’ (1:7). He must be ‘hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined’ (1:8). And he must hold firmly to the true message so that he can encourage believers and answer those who oppose it (1:9).

The list closely matches 1 Timothy 3, and the questions it raises are the same: how churches today are ordered, what ‘the husband of but one wife’ means, whether ‘children who are believers’ means children who profess faith or children who are faithful and well behaved, and whether the office is open to women. The book page on 1 Timothy and the notes on Titus 1 set out the views. These notes do not choose.

What every reading shares is that character comes before gifting. A gifted leader who is violent, greedy, harsh or proud does not meet Paul's standard. And nothing in this list shields a leader who does harm.

parts.h: ‘The circumcision group’ and the Cretan saying (1:10-16)
parts.body:
Paul says that ‘many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision’ (1:10). They ‘undermine entire households’ for money (1:11), and teach ‘Jewish myths’ and ‘the commands of men’ (1:14), it seems including rules about what is clean and unclean (1:15).

This was a dispute among people inside the church. ‘Those of the circumcision’ were most likely Jewish believers, or teachers close to them, who pressed parts of the law on Gentile believers. Paul himself was a Jew. Titus, a Gentile, had been the test case of whether Gentile believers must be circumcised (Galatians 2:3). Paul's quarrel is with a teaching that added rules to grace and took money for it. It is not with Jews, not with Judaism, and not with the law God gave, which Paul calls holy (Romans 7:12). For centuries some Christians used words like these to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why.

Then Paul quotes a Cretan: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons” (1:12). Ancient tradition says the line came from Epimenides, a Cretan poet of about the 500s BC; its first words also appear in the poet Callimachus. Other Greeks mocked Cretans for claiming that the tomb of Zeus was on their island, and even made a verb from the island's name meaning ‘to lie’.

Paul uses the line with some irony, turning a Cretan's own words against particular teachers who were lying for gain. His aim is that they ‘will be sound in the faith’ (1:13). He is not passing a verdict on every Cretan. He had worked among Cretans, and the church on Crete was made of them. The God of this letter is the one ‘who cannot lie’ (1:2), and he loves the Cretans enough to send them elders.

This verse must never be used to justify contempt for any people, nation or race, or to say that some group is liars or lazy by nature. People have done that with it, and it is wrong. The gospel Paul preached on Crete says that ‘at one time we too were foolish’ (3:3), all of us, and that God saved us by mercy.

parts.h: Women, men and slaves (2:1-10): what all agree, and how Christians differ
parts.body:
Chapter 2 goes through the church group by group. Older men are to be self-controlled and sound in faith and love. Older women are to be ‘teachers of good’ who train the younger women ‘to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited’ (2:4-5). Younger men are to be self-controlled, and Titus an example. And ‘slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything’ (2:9).

Notice the reason Paul gives again and again: so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5), so that opponents will have nothing bad to say (2:8), so that slaves will ‘adorn the teaching about God our Savior’ (2:10). Outsiders watched Christian households closely, and critics said the new faith disrupted families. Paul wants the church's homes to make the gospel beautiful. Notice too that older women are given real teaching work, and that every group, men and women alike, is called to the same self-control.

On wives and husbands, Christians who share the same faith read verse 5 differently, and it is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith. Complementarians hold that a wife's submission to her husband is a lasting pattern for Christian marriage, given freely, never taken, and that a husband's headship means self-giving love, as Ephesians 5:22-33 says. Egalitarians hold that Paul is applying the gospel within the household customs of his day for the sake of the gospel's good name, that Ephesians 5:21 begins with mutual submission, and that where culture no longer sees a partnership of equals as a disgrace, the same concern points to marriages of mutual submission. These notes do not choose. Nothing here licenses abuse. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

On slaves, Paul does not command the end of slavery here, and that should not be softened. But he speaks to slaves as people who can ‘adorn the teaching about God’, in a world that called them property. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used verses like these to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. The notes on chapter 2 say more.

parts.h: Grace that trains, and ‘our great God and Savior’ (2:11-14)
parts.body:
“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:11-13).

Grace here is not only pardon. It is a teacher. The word for ‘instructs’ is the word for bringing up a child. Grace forgives, and then grace trains, patiently, the way a good parent trains a child.

The Christian life sits between two appearings. Grace has appeared, in Christ's first coming. And believers wait for ‘the glorious appearance’ of Christ when he returns. The Greek word gives English the word ‘epiphany’; it was used for a god showing himself or a ruler arriving in a city.

Then comes the phrase ‘our great God and Savior Jesus Christ’. Most translations, the BSB among them, and most readers take it as one person: Jesus Christ is our great God and Savior. With the church in every age, these notes confess that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, one with the Father. That confession does not rest on this verse alone (John 1:1; 20:28; Hebrews 1:8).

And why did he come? “He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds” (2:14). ‘His own possession’ is the language God used of Israel at Sinai. Through Christ, Gentiles like the Cretans are welcomed into that people.

parts.h: Saved by mercy; ‘the washing of new birth’ (3:3-7)
parts.body:
Paul reminds the believers where they came from. “For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another” (3:3). Notice ‘we’. Paul does not stand outside the list.

Then comes the turn. “But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life” (3:4-7).

In these few lines the Father, the Spirit and the Son act together in one rescue: God our Savior saves, the Holy Spirit renews, and Jesus Christ pours out the Spirit. It is the pattern the church confesses as the Trinity. And all of it rests on God's mercy, not on anything we did.

What is ‘the washing of new birth’? Christians read it in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians generally hold that it speaks of baptism, through which God truly gives new birth. Reformed and Presbyterian Christians often see baptism here as a sign and seal of the new birth the Spirit works. Baptists and many other evangelicals read the washing as the Spirit's inward cleansing, pictured with water, and see baptism as the outward sign of what has already happened. These notes do not choose. All agree on what the verse plainly says: salvation comes by God's mercy, not our deeds, and the Holy Spirit is the one who makes us new.

parts.h: Good neighbours, and the divisive person (3:1-2, 8-11)
parts.body:
Paul asks believers ‘to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone’ (3:1-2). Small Christian groups met privately and refused the gods of their neighbours, so they were easily suspected. Paul wants them known for good conduct toward everyone.

This is not a lesson for any party. Christians are to pray for and respect those who govern, whoever they are. And the rest of the Bible sets limits: when rulers forbade the apostles to preach, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). The notes on Romans 13 set out how Christians differ on when disobedience is right.

Then Paul tells Titus to avoid ‘foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law’ (3:9), and: “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition” (3:10). The word for ‘divisive’ later gave English the word ‘heretic’, but here it describes behaviour: a person who keeps stirring up factions and quarrels. Paul gives two warnings first. Patience comes before refusal.

This verse must never be used against someone who has been harmed and speaks up, or against someone who asks honest questions or tells the truth. A person who reports abuse is not ‘divisive’. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities. The notes on chapter 3 say more.

God ‘who cannot lie’ (1:2) is the God of Numbers: “God is not a man, that He should lie” (Numbers 23:19).

‘A people for His own possession’ (2:14) is what God called Israel at Sinai: “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations” (Exodus 19:5), and “The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession” (Deuteronomy 7:6).

‘The kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind’ (3:4) echoes God's own name as he told it to Moses: “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

‘The washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit’ (3:5) recalls Ezekiel's promise: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25), and “I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27). And the Spirit ‘poured out … abundantly’ (3:6) recalls Joel: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28).

And the call to be good neighbours in a city that did not share the faith sounds like Jeremiah's letter to the exiles: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7).

It is not a licence for contempt of any people. The Cretan saying (1:12) was aimed at particular teachers, and the letter's own gospel puts every reader in the list of the foolish and lost (3:3).

It is not against the Jewish people. ‘Those of the circumcision’ were teachers in a dispute among believers, and Paul was a Jew.

It is not a defence of slavery, and it is not a rule for employment. A worker is not property, and no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.

It is not a licence for abuse in marriage or anywhere else, and it does not ask anyone to stay in danger.

It is not a way to silence the harmed. ‘Reject a divisive man’ (3:10) is about people who keep stirring up factions, never about people who report wrong.

It is not salvation by good works. ‘Not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy’ (3:5). Good works are the fruit of grace, never its price.

And it is not a lesson for any party. Respect for rulers is asked of believers under every government.

Read it in one sitting, and read it beside 1 Timothy. Notice what is the same, elders, false teachers, sound teaching, and what is different: younger churches, plainer instructions, and a strong concern for how outsiders see the church.

Watch for the phrase ‘good works’ in every chapter (1:16; 2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14), and for the little words ‘so that’, which tell you why Paul asks what he asks (2:5, 8, 10).

Read the two gospel summaries (2:11-14 and 3:4-7) slowly. Everything else in the letter rests on them.

Where the letter is debated, on who wrote it, on elders, on wives and husbands, on baptism, read the case for more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And let the letter ask you its questions. Does what you believe show up in how you live? Is your home a place that makes the gospel attractive? Do you remember what you were before grace found you? And are you devoted to meeting the pressing needs of others (3:14)?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: Elders: ‘the husband of but one wife’ and ‘children who are believers’. The readings, and character first.
‘Those of the circumcision.’ A dispute among believers, never a word against the Jewish people.
‘Cretans are always liars.’ A Cretan poet quoted against particular teachers, and never a licence for contempt of any people.
Older and younger women, and ‘submissive to their own husbands’. What all agree, both readings, and safety first.
Slaves and masters. Why Paul did not command the end of slavery, and the misuse of these verses.
‘Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.’ Christ's deity confessed.
‘Submit to rulers and authorities.’ Respect for every government, its limits, and no party lesson.
‘The washing of new birth.’ How churches read it of baptism, each fairly.
‘Reject a divisive man.’ Never a way to silence the harmed.

words.line: Greek presbuteros and episkopos. In Titus the same leaders, it seems (1:5, 7).
Greek oikonomos, the manager of a household for its owner. Leaders do not own the church; they manage it for God (1:7).
Healthy. Teaching that makes people well (1:9, 13; 2:1-2).
Greek sōphrōn, a sound, steady mind that rules its desires. Asked of every group in chapter 2.
Greek apseudēs, found only here (1:2). Set against the Cretan saying of 1:12.
Greek paideuō, the word for bringing up a child. Grace is the teacher (2:12).
Greek epiphaneia, the source of ‘epiphany’. Used for a god showing himself or a ruler arriving (2:13).
Greek periousios, found only here. God's word for Israel at Sinai (2:14; Exodus 19:5).
Greek palingenesia, becoming again. In Matthew 19:28 it names the renewal of all things (3:5).
Greek philanthrōpia, the root of ‘philanthropy’, a virtue praised in kings. Here it is God's (3:4).
Greek hairetikos, used only here. A person who makes factions, the later source of ‘heretic’ (3:10).

timeline.what: Octavian, later the emperor Augustus, wins the sea battle of Actium and founds Nicopolis nearby to mark it.
At Pentecost, Cretans are among the crowd in Jerusalem who hear the apostles (Acts 2:11).

timeline.when: About AD 48 to 50, on many readings
timeline.what: Titus goes up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas and is not made to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3).
Paul sends Titus to Corinth. Titus meets Paul in Macedonia with good news (2 Corinthians 7:6-7).
Paul's ship, carrying him as a prisoner, shelters at Fair Havens on Crete's south coast (Acts 27:7-13).
Paul under guard in Rome for two years, where Acts ends (Acts 28:30-31).

timeline.when: About AD 62 to 64, if Paul wrote it
timeline.what: Released, Paul works on Crete with Titus, leaves him there, and writes this letter, planning to winter at Nicopolis.

timeline.when: About AD 80 to 110, on another view
timeline.what: Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters usually date them here.
Titus goes to Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast (2 Timothy 4:10).

places.name: Crete
places.line: The island where Paul left Titus to appoint elders in every town (1:5). The mark is Fair Havens on its south coast, where Paul's ship once sheltered (Acts 27:8).

places.name: Nicopolis
places.line: A city on the west coast of Greece, founded by Augustus after Actium. Paul planned to winter here and asked Titus to come (3:12). Most scholars think this is the Nicopolis he meant.

teaching.mapNote: Crete lies south of the Aegean Sea. Nicopolis, where Paul planned to spend the winter, is on the western coast of Greece, facing Italy across the sea.
